video.title: The Magic of the Non-Dominant Side on the Forehand

classification.reason: The coach provides two specific actionable cues to internalize non-dominant side control ('hold the shoulder' and feel like you are pressing back in across the body).

problem.title_as_question: How does the non-dominant side work on the forehand to maintain balance and elbow tuck?
problem.definition: Players often fail to tuck the non-dominant elbow or maintain balance through the follow-through because they do not actively press the non-dominant side back across the body against rotational momentum.

quotes.text: Look at the forehand K ends this point with. Strange, right? His arms actually crossed.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Well, the left side of your chest, it actually presses back across the body on every forehand, but normally you can't see it
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: because that initial rotational explosion that starts the swing, it sends the left side out with momentum and then that pressing action where the left side presses back in.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The net effect is just this elbow tuck rather than an actual press back across because that outward vector is getting cancelled out by the inward vector.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now, if you didn't press at all though, it would look like this. And all of the sudden, oh, okay, you can see that doesn't look like a very well balanced forehand.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And that inward pressing action is necessary to get that tucked elbow position that you see everyone play the forehand in.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Lorenzo Mousetti is a great one to look at for this because he occasionally hits these running down the line forehand winners.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And because he cuts off that rotation a little bit early on those to hit that down the line target, you can actually see that left arm across pressing action in the follow through.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: You can actually see that hand appear on the other side of his torso.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, there are two cues, two ways to internalize this depending on what feels more intuitive for you.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: One is the literal action that's happening, which is hold the shoulder. So, as you swing, we don't want to let this happen. We want to hold that shoulder.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The second one, and this is my favorite because I think more people find it intuitive, is it will feel like you're pressing like this even on your regular forehands where rotation cancels out most of that inwards momentum.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And that's because without pressing, you get this. And that pressing action for most people, their brain thinks it's doing this even if it's doing this.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So now that we've got that, let's just watch one more point from Kenya Jakori and watch how expertly he uses his left side to control his forehands and overheads.
quotes.speaker: coach

symptoms.description: The forehand finish loses balance and the non-dominant arm flies open rather than tucking in.
The non-dominant elbow fails to tuck tightly against the ribs during follow-through.

causes.statement: The left side of the chest must actively press back across the body inward to counterbalance rotation and tuck the elbow.
The initial rotational explosion that starts the forward swing naturally sends the non-dominant side outward with momentum.
Failing to exert an inward pressing action with the non-dominant side leaves the outward momentum unchecked, ruining stroke balance.

angles.summary: The tucked elbow position is the net vector result of outward momentum from torso rotation being cancelled out by active inward pressing of the non-dominant chest.
Musetti's running down-the-line forehands expose the inward pressing action because he cuts off body rotation early, making his non-dominant hand visibly emerge on the opposite side of his torso.
Even though full rotation visually cancels out visible arm crossing, the internal feeling in the brain should still be actively pressing across.

solutions.summary: Use the cue 'hold the shoulder' as you swing to prevent the non-dominant side from flying open.
Feel like you are actively pressing the non-dominant arm across the chest even on normal forehands where rotation cancels out the visual motion.
